title: A Simple Way To Teach Compelling Lessons
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a single, focused strategy for making lessons more engaging: stop leading with the "what" of a lesson and instead lead with the benefit — why it's worth learning. He argues that announcing the topic ("today we're going to learn how to divide fractions") is inherently boring and fails to resonate, making sustained attention a struggle for many students. Instead, he recommends teachers identify at least one genuine benefit, however creative or tangential, and use it as the lesson's opening hook, giving playful example phrasings for a math lesson. He acknowledges math often poses the greatest challenge for finding an appealing benefit but insists one always exists. The habit, he says, becomes easier with practice until benefits start to "jump out" during lesson planning, ultimately capturing student interest lesson after lesson.
points: Lead lesson introductions with the benefit — why the material is worth learning — rather than simply stating the topic.
Stating the bare topic ("today we're learning X") is inherently unengaging and rarely resonates with students.
Benefits can be playful, humorous, or only tangentially related to the content, as long as they're genuinely interesting.
Finding a lesson's "one benefit" becomes easier with repeated practice during lesson planning.
quotes: The ability to get your students to want to listen and pay attention plays a critical role in curbing misbehavior.
But the problem with this approach is that the ‘what’ is boring . It’s groan inducing. It rarely, if ever, makes a connection with students.
So instead of focusing on ‘what’ you’re going to teach, focus on what’s in it for them. Focus on why it’s worth learning.
I’m going to show you a cool trick to dividing fractions today that you’re not going to believe!

Just think about what is—or can be—fun or weird or scary or fascinating or gross or surprising or helpful or otherwise noteworthy about your topic, and then sell it to your students during your introduction.
Explain what’s in it for them. Tell them why the lesson is worth their time.
